item.title: The Traitors of Tranquillien
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The pamphlets were the first thing to burn. They always are. Laotou walked into Tranquillien at dusk to find the Twilight’s Blade nailing its gospel to every post and doorframe in town, and the monk, who has never once been persuaded by a pamphlet, set about tearing them down.
item.content:encoded:
The pamphlets were the first thing to burn. They always are. Laotou walked into Tranquillien at dusk to find the Twilight’s Blade nailing its gospel to every post and doorframe in town, and the monk, who has never once been persuaded by a pamphlet, set about tearing them down.

The cult had been living here a long while, it turned out. Their cover was blown now, so they had stopped pretending and started fighting in the open, which is the only honest thing a cult ever does. Voidlings crawled out from between the houses. Obelisks hummed in the square. There were supply crates to smash and effigies to break, and Laotou broke them, one after another, with the patient rhythm of someone sweeping a floor.

Arator stood among the wreckage and would not let the town fall. The governor had made his terms plain: join the Blade or be executed. So while the fighting went on, the Pandaren went door to door pulling frightened elves out of the line of fire. Healers are good at this part. Nobody writes songs about it, but nobody who was carried out of a burning house forgets who did the carrying.

Then came the ugly work. The traitors of Tranquillien were not strangers. Ranger Lethvalin. Matron Narsilla. Guard Captain Leonic. Names the town had trusted for years, the sort of people who teach the young ones their trade and keep the watch at night. All three wore the Blade’s colors under their cloaks. The chronicler has seen this before, in Lordaeron, in Stormwind, in every city that thought itself too proud to rot. The rot never comes from outside. Laotou cut them down, and Tranquillien was quieter afterward, though not in any way that felt like peace.

From the traitors’ leavings the monk took up a Twilight Agitator’s Stave, held it for the space of a breath, and set it down again in favor of the old Mistdancer Staff. The chronicler approves. A healer should not carry a weapon that was made to stir up crowds.

Magister Umbric had gone missing in the confusion, off chasing Antenorian, the governor who had sold the town. Umbric had his reasons. Kasiea was dead, her research torn from her body, and grief makes a man careless about what waits around corners. Laotou found the trail through a secretary named Faloria, who had a jeweled key and a strongbox and a great deal to answer for. Inside the box were plans of infiltration and a stack of spare pamphlets. Cults are nothing if not well stocked.

Umbric was alive. Angry, but alive.

The cult had marked other places on its maps, and one of them was Windrunner Village, the old seat of the family whose name still makes rangers stand a little straighter. So the road went on, past the Hollow Grove, to a village too quiet for anyone’s comfort. Laotou went about waking the old ranger constructs that slump at its borders, arcane golems gone to rust and moss, and set them back on their feet to stand guard and sniff out snakes in the grass. The monk came away from it with a pair of tights once tailored for a Twilight spy. Spoils are spoils. The chronicler does not ask.

Upstairs in the village, Umbric tried one last ritual. Arator talked. Laotou carried four void shards out of the balconies and fed them, one by one, into the dark sphere at the center of the room, and watched it swell with each. Whatever Umbric learned there, he did not like it. The monk wore a depleted voidshard ring away from that room and gathered a mote of light on the way out, as if the world were trying to even the scales.

Then south, to the Ruins of Deatholme, where Dar’Khan Drathir once kept house for the Scourge and where nothing good has grown since. The Twilight’s Blade has chosen it for a fortress. Fitting, Umbric said. Valeera Sanguinar was waiting there, quiet as a knife in a sleeve. She had tracked Antenorian to a cavern beneath the ruins.

He has gone in. Laotou has not, yet. The cavern waits, and so does the governor, and so do the missing pages of a dead woman’s notes.

item.title: What Are People Rolling in WoW Forever? X vs Bluesky
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: WoW Forever launches on November 4, 2026, and name reservation opens just before that. Like a lot of you, I’ve spent the beta weeks reading everyone’s “here’s my main” posts and wondering which way the crowd is going. Horde or Alliance? PvP or RP? How many Undead Paladins is Azeroth about to get?
item.content:encoded:
WoW Forever launches on November 4, 2026, and name reservation opens just before that. Like a lot of you, I’ve spent the beta weeks reading everyone’s “here’s my main” posts and wondering which way the crowd is going. Horde or Alliance? PvP or RP? How many Undead Paladins is Azeroth about to get?

So I went and counted. I read through public posts on X and Bluesky from the start of the beta to now and tallied what people said they’re planning to play. I kept the two networks separate, because it turns out they really don’t agree.

How I collected the data

  • Date range: September 17, 2026 (beta launch day) through October 25, 2026.
  • Where: X, using search of public posts, and Bluesky, using its public search. I didn’t sign in to either one.
  • What counted: only clear statements about the person’s own choice, like “I’m maining a Tauren Druid.” Questions, jokes, ads, bots, news, guides and “still deciding” posts were skipped.
  • One vote per person: each person counts once, by their stated main. Alts are ignored. If someone only mentioned a character they played in the beta and never stated a plan, I counted that, but treated it as weaker evidence.
  • How much:
    • X: about 35 searches turned up 562 posts. I read 483 of them closely and counted 226 people.
    • Bluesky: I scanned 6,037 posts, read 239 that talked about picks, and counted 105 people.

Known gaps

  • The X giveaway thread. One X giveaway asked people to comment the class they’re playing. That gave me 41 class-only replies, but they came with a prize attached. I show the X class numbers with and without them.
  • Partial reply threads on X. X search only returns part of big reply threads. The giveaway had 864 replies, and search found about 44 of them.
  • Bluesky paging. Bluesky’s public search wouldn’t go past the first page of results. I searched in two-day windows and took the first page of each, so some posts were missed.
  • Not a random sample. These are English posts from people who chose to share their pick. Very few people named a ruleset or a spec, so treat those numbers as hints.

Bluesky barely moved. It was Horde-heavy with Undead and Tauren on top in both periods. The main change is rulesets: more people named one later on, and RP-PvP only shows up after October 22. Two of the 105 people had no post date I could place in either period, so the two columns add up to 103.

A few differences stand out.

Bluesky is much more Horde. About three out of four Bluesky players who named a faction picked Horde. On X it’s closer to a coin flip, and it was dead even in recent weeks. Bluesky also stayed steady over time, while X drifted toward Alliance.

Humans are nearly absent on Bluesky. Human is the second most named race on X, but only 2 people on Bluesky picked one. Alliance players on Bluesky lean Night Elf instead.

Paladin leads on X, Druid on Bluesky. Both love the Undead Paladin, but beyond that X has more Human Paladins and Hunters. Bluesky leans toward Tauren Druids, Tauren Warriors and Troll Warlocks.

Rulesets split the clearest. X players who named a ruleset mostly said PvP. On Bluesky, almost nobody did; people there talked about Normal and RP. The ruleset numbers are small on both sides, though.

Why the difference? I can only guess. Bluesky’s WoW crowd seems to have a lot of artists, roleplayers and VTubers, the kind of folks who love Tauren and Night Elves and sit out world PvP. X has more streamers, guild recruiters and competitive players, and when big guilds go Alliance, that shows up there first. And with 105 people on Bluesky, a single friend group can tilt the results.

For a different angle, the beta census counted actual beta characters, not posts. NayKu’s count of 1,003,125 characters came out Alliance 50.4% / Horde 49.6%, with Undead the top race (16.6%), Hunter the top class (15.6%) and Undead Paladin the top combo (5.8%). The ClassicPlus census of October 16 also showed factions about even. X lines up with that much more closely than Bluesky does.

Wrapping up

My takeaway is that the Undead Paladin is everywhere, factions will probably be fine, and which network you hang out on changes what “everyone” seems to be playing. If you only read Bluesky, you’d think Stormwind will be a ghost town. Based on the census, it won’t be.

As for me, I’m leaning Dwarf Enhancement Shaman for Forever. On X that put me in a small club of three Dwarf Shamans. On Bluesky, nobody named one at all. I’ll see you on November 4. Tell me what you’re rolling.

item.title: Through the Gates of Zul’Aman
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The Gates of Zul’Aman have kept elves out for longer than most kingdoms have kept anything. That evening they opened for a Kul Tiran who smelled of tar and salt, and the trolls on the other side were not sure whether to thank him or count their silverware.
item.content:encoded:
The Gates of Zul’Aman have kept elves out for longer than most kingdoms have kept anything. That evening they opened for a Kul Tiran who smelled of tar and salt, and the trolls on the other side were not sure whether to thank him or count their silverware.

It began at the Amani Pass, where Lady Liadrin and her Blood Knights hold the road between Eversong and the troll lands. The Amani had surrendered the lightwood they took from the elves, but Zul’jan, who led that raid, never went home. He lingered at the gates with his warriors, and Liadrin, who had run out of patience with him, sent Burrly to try diplomacy instead. The talk was cut short when a Void beast came howling out of the shadows, and the matter of who was angrier at whom was set aside so everyone could kill it. Burrly helped. When the dust settled, the elves learned that Zul’jan does not lead the Amani at all. His sister does. Her name is Zul’jarra, granddaughter of Zul’jin himself, and Liadrin said, with an elf’s gift for understatement, that this might be worse.

Liadrin meant to talk her way through the gate, and told him to follow her lead. Before that was settled, Burrly went down. On the western edge of Zul’Aman lies a second Atal’Aman, a delve, where the Delvers send their braver and less sensible recruits. Valeera Sanguinar walked beside him, the same quiet blade from the Darkway and the Plaza. Somewhere in the dark he took up the Delvers’ call for this place. He gathered small blessings off the fallen, as is his habit: a Boon of Possibilities, a Boon of Potency, a Boon of Power. At one point he fell a very long way and got up again, which a man should be allowed to brag about.

At the bottom waited the Disciple of Vashnik, a priest of the serpent-cult that calls itself the Children of Ula’tek, who spits venom and calls slimes out of the floor. The chronicler was not down there and will not invent the blows. The record says only that the Disciple fell, and Burrly walked out with a Hex Loop on one finger and a Depleted Voidshard Ring on the other. A man in a troll city wearing a hex ring. Bold. Valeera left at the surface, as she always does, without farewell.

Liadrin got her passage. Zul’jarra let the two of them through, though not the Blood Knights, and the reason was plain enough: the Twilight’s Blade had come for Atal’Aman, the old temple city, under a general named Mor’duun, and the Amani had nobody else to ask. Liadrin admitted that no one from Eversong had set foot on that side of the border in years, then told Burrly not to turn his back on his hosts. The Amani, presumably, were telling each other the same thing. Somewhere in that crossing he felt it again, the slow thickening of arm and back that comes from surviving one more thing that meant to kill him. Another rung. The ladder does not care which side of the border you stand on.

Then up into the city proper, where the drums are. Zul’jarra had asked him to find Atal’Aman’s great war drums and beat them, to call the Witherbark, the Revantusk and the Shadowpine to the fight, and to tell the civilians to fall back to the Altar of Malacrass. Liadrin, meanwhile, wanted the Amani to see how efficiently outsiders can kill shadows. So Burrly did both. He sounded the drums and cut down the Void-things in the streets, and Zul’jarra noticed. The Amani paid him in a pair of Twilightbreaker’s Gauntlets, which he buckled on before the troll finished speaking.

Then he did a strange thing. He left. A call came from the far side of the world, from the ruined coast of Gilneas, where Alliance and Horde have been fighting over mines and lighthouses since the Wall fell. He answered it. It went badly. A hunter called Marylou put him in the dirt at the Mines, then again at the Waterworks, then a third time on the Gilnean Coast. A mage called Coujaa did it twice more near the end, the last time at the Lighthouse. By the chronicler’s count he died ten times in a quarter of an hour, and the Horde carried the day. War is a ledger, and that night the Kul Tiran’s column was red.

He came back to Zul’Aman and stood at the Altar of Malacrass, where the Amani have been told to gather, with Swiftclaw Terrace still full of Twilight soldiers and three Amani elders still somewhere in the city who have not answered the drums. Zul’jarra wants them found. One of them is her uncle, an old loa speaker who, she warns, may need special persuasion to leave.

The chronicler has known a few old men like that. They usually stay until the roof comes down.

item.title: The Gladius of Parhelion Plaza
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The Void came for the Sunwell again, the way it always does, and this time it brought a general. Gladius Slaurna held the battlements of Parhelion Plaza with Voidcallers at his feet, ready to feed them to the dark for a little more strength. Then a Kul Tiran came down the stairs, smelling faintly of tar and harbor, and the general’s evening got considerably worse.
item.content:encoded:
The Void came for the Sunwell again, the way it always does, and this time it brought a general. Gladius Slaurna held the battlements of Parhelion Plaza with Voidcallers at his feet, ready to feed them to the dark for a little more strength. Then a Kul Tiran came down the stairs, smelling faintly of tar and harbor, and the general’s evening got considerably worse.

Burrly had started humbly enough. A quick crossing to the Trading Post in Stormwind City, where Tawny Seabraid hands out each month’s tender. Then back to Silvermoon, where Magister Astalor Bloodsworn keeps a hunt table in his sanctum and a list of names. The first he gave Burrly was Grothoz, the Burning Shadow: an ogre of the Twilight’s Blade and, by Astalor’s account, the brains of a particularly stupid cabal. The magister calls it Prey. The elves have a gift for making murder sound like a hobby.

Somewhere on the Shining Span, the great bridge from the city to the Isle of Quel’Danas, he also acquired a guild. Azeroth Morning Radio took him on as a Commoner. Burrly has never needed a title. He has needed someone to drink with. Now he has a roster of them.

He went into the Plaza alone. The Delvers had posted their call in Silvermoon: Quel’Danas is under attack by the Void once more, and any who can should help stem the tide. So he stemmed it. The halls gave up small mercies: a Boon of Vigor, a Boon of Possibilities, another Boon of Vigor, a Boon of Fortitude, a Boon of Potency. The elves name their blessings like perfume. A warrior uses them like bandages.

Then Slaurna himself, one of the hardest things waiting in any of these delves. The chronicler was not in the room and will not invent the blows, but the record is clear about the ending. The Gladius fell, and Burrly stood over him on the Sunwell’s own battlements, breathing hard and very much alive. Only then does the record put Valeera Sanguinar at his side, the blood elf assassin who walks the delves with anyone foolish enough to enter them. What she did before that, the record does not say. She would prefer it that way.

The Plaza’s chest paid in strange coin. A Spark of Tides, the kind of thing master crafters build their finest work around. A Primeval Arcane Remnant, humming with something older than anyone cares to guess. A jeweler’s design for a replica Haranir mural. And a pair of Pledgebearer’s Pauldrons. He put them on. He looked at himself. Moments later he took them off and went back to his old Front-Line Shoulders of the Aurora. Some men know their own shape. The chronicler respects that more than most victories.

Valeera left at the threshold without a word. She always does.

Back at the Delver’s Headquarters in Silvermoon, he laid the Remnant before Naleidea Rivergleam, who called it an extraordinary find and asked for more. Then he collected on the Delvers’ call. Somewhere between the praise and the purse he felt it again: that slow thickening of shoulder and spine that only comes from surviving things that should have killed you. Another rung. The ladder does not care.

Then out along the Path of Dawn into Eversong Woods, after Grothoz. And here the chronicle owes the truth. At Lightbloom Ath’Ran, where Light-fed overgrowth has swallowed the old Scorched Grove and nothing grows politely anymore, a stranger called Headhaunta caught him with a lance of Dawnlight and put him in the grass. Not a beast. Not a shadow. Another hunter, who saw a Kul Tiran and saw a trophy. Burrly lay among the flowers for a while and considered his choices.

He came back. Of course he did. He pried ore from the stone, picked Motes of Light out of the ground like a man collecting teeth after a brawl, and kept at the hunt until the ogre had nowhere left to hide. Grothoz, the Burning Shadow, burns no more. In Astalor’s Sanctum the magister paid him in gold, another Spark of Tides, an Aspiring Preyhunter’s Chest, and the Preyhunter’s Polished Vambraces, which he buckled on before the ink on the receipt was dry. He sold the rest, and his purse went home heavier than it had any right to be.

The last thing he did before the lamps went down was take another name: Thornspeaker Edgath, a druid who turns the wild on enemies and innocents alike. It is time, says Astalor, to clip this thorn. Burrly did not argue.

And somewhere in Eversong, Headhaunta is still walking around with a story about the day they killed a sailor. Stories like that have a way of getting a second chapter.

item.title: How My Azeroth Life is made: from a WoW addon to a podcast
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: This post is also on the Nine Point Labs blog.
item.content:encoded:
This post is also on the Nine Point Labs blog.

If you’ve been reading the Chronicler’s tales here, you may have wondered where they come from. And if you’ve seen the new My Azeroth Life podcast, you may have wondered who is doing the voices. This is the behind-the-scenes post.

The short answer: every story here starts with something I really did in World of Warcraft. AI does the writing and the narration, and I read every post and listen to every episode before it goes up. The whole site, podcast included, is published by folderblog, the small blog engine I make at Nine Point Labs.

The road from a play session to an episode

World of Warcraft, with the StoryTracker addon
    |  log out or /reload: the addon saves its notes
    v
Companion script: one file of new events per character
    |  every morning
    v
AI writes a draft post in the Chronicler's voice
    |  I read it and approve it
    v
folderblog publishes it here on My Azeroth Life
    |
    v
Claude writes a script, ElevenLabs voices it, ffmpeg mixes it
    |  I listen, then say yes
    v
folderblog publishes the episode to the podcast feed

The addon: StoryTracker

While I play, an addon I wrote called StoryTracker quietly takes notes. It records the quests I pick up and turn in, every zone I walk into, levels gained, deaths (where, and what did it), rare and better loot, reputation changes, dungeon bosses, profession skill-ups, gold earned and spent, notable kills, groups and guilds, and how long each session lasted.

WoW only lets an addon save to disk when you log out or /reload, so the notes are written at the end of each session. If you’d like to try it, both versions are free on GitHub: StoryTracker for WoW Forever and StoryTracker for Retail.

From notes to a Chronicler’s tale

A small script on my computer reads those notes, picks out only what is new since last time, and sorts it by character and by game, so Retail and Forever adventures never get mixed up.

Every morning, if anyone has been out adventuring, an AI agent reads the new events along with a voice guide and writes a post as the Chronicler: a weathered scribe who has followed adventurers across Azeroth for decades and is no longer impressed by much. The guide asks for real weight when a moment earns it, honest grit when things go wrong, and a dry smirk the rest of the time. Game events become world events, so a death has a repair bill and a level-up feels like surviving something that should have killed you.

The post lands in a drafts folder, tagged with the game version, the character and their class. Then I read it from top to bottom. Only when I’m happy with it does it move to the published posts.

How folderblog runs the site

folderblog watches a folder on my computer. Each post is a plain text file, and putting a file in the posts folder is all it takes: a few seconds later the post is live here. A few of the things it does for this site:

  • Drafts stay on my computer until I approve them.
  • Tags get their own pages, so you can read only Burrly’s story or only Laotou’s.
  • The parchment theme you’re looking at is a custom theme. folderblog themes are simple templates, which made it easy to build with an AI coding assistant.
  • Safe publishing. If something is wrong with a build, the site keeps the last good version instead of breaking.
  • A built-in checker (folderblog check) catches broken links and feed problems before you’d ever see them.

Turning the stories into audio

Once there are enough tales, Claude, an AI coding assistant running on my computer, turns them into an episode. It writes a script from the posts, split into chapters, with notes on the background sounds, the effects, and how each line should be performed.

Every character gets their own narrator, designed with ElevenLabs and then kept for good:

  • Laotou, the Pandaren monk, is told by an old lorewalker over a pot of tea, slow and wry.
  • Burrly, the Kul Tiran warrior, is told by an old sea captain in a Boralus tavern, fast and loud, because most of his story is him charging at things.

The narration uses ElevenLabs’ most expressive voice model, which can be told to sound intense, dry or quiet line by line. Music and sound effects are made with ElevenLabs too: a theme for each show, background music that shifts with the scene (with proper battle music for the fights), a gong between Laotou’s chapters, a ship’s bell and war drum between Burrly’s, and plenty of clashing steel and tavern noise. Names get special care. Laotou is said “Lau-Toe”, and Burrly is said just like “burly”.

Then everything is mixed together. The music dips whenever the narrator speaks, the effects land between lines, the volume is set to a normal podcast level, and chapter markers are added so you can skip around. Every line is run back through speech-to-text and compared with the script to catch anything missing or made up, and then I listen to the whole episode myself. All the music and effects are kept in a library and reused, so each character’s world keeps sounding the same.

How folderblog runs the podcast

The podcast lives in the same blog. Each episode is a folder with its show notes, the audio and a list of chapters, and folderblog builds:

  • The podcast page with a Subscribe box, and a page for each episode with a player and clickable chapters.
  • Its own feed at myazerothlife.com/podcast/feed.xml, separate from the blog’s feed, so you can follow the audio without the posts or the other way around.
  • Audio hosted on Cloudflare R2. folderblog uploads each episode, checks that it is really online, and only then adds it to the feed.
  • Draft episodes that stay private until I’ve listened and said yes.

What’s coming

From now on there are up to two episodes a week in the same feed:

  • The Retail show on Sunday nights.
  • The Forever show on Monday nights, starting after WoW Forever launches on November 4.

Each one covers every character who had an adventure that week, with a short transition between them, and is tagged by game. If nobody played that version that week, there’s simply no show. Every character keeps their narrator, so a familiar voice will always be telling a familiar hero’s story.

Have a listen

  • Episode 1: The Chronicle of Laotou, 23 minutes in 5 chapters
  • Episode 2: The Chronicle of Burrly, 26 minutes in 8 chapters
  • Add the feed to your podcast app: https://myazerothlife.com/podcast/feed.xml

Thanks for reading, and for listening. If you have a favorite moment, or a character you’d like to hear more of, I’d love to know.

item.title: My WoW Forever beta report card
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Blizzard handed out beta stats for WoW Forever, and mine read less like a report card and more like evidence.
item.content:encoded:
Blizzard handed out beta stats for WoW Forever, and mine read less like a report card and more like evidence.

30 characters played, 99th percentile. Ninety-nine percent of beta testers showed more restraint than I did. In my defense, every class looked fun, every race has a great starting zone, and the character creation screen is right there.

107 levels gained, 90th percentile. Spread across 30 characters, that comes to about three and a half levels each. A lot of them never made it past the first quest hub. They live on in my character list, forever level 4 and full of promise.

128 boars killed, 79th percentile. If you were a boar in Durotar or Dun Morogh during the beta, I’m sorry. Mostly. You dropped good meat.

337 gathering actions, 65th percentile. Finally, a stat where I’m merely average. It’s hard to keep a gathering profession going when you roll a new character before the first herb respawns.

WoW Forever launches November 4. I’m told a sensible person picks a main. I’ll let you know how that goes.

item.title: The Scarab at Runestone Falithas
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The scarab was fat with something that wasn’t its own. That was the first thing anyone would have noticed, if anyone had been watching besides the chronicler. An Engorged Scarab, the elves of Eversong call them, which is a polite word for a beetle that has been drinking from the wrong well.
